notes: Introduce yourself and KAVACH. The project connects login events to security alerts and makes the underlying evidence available during an investigation.
Start with a simple example. A failed password might be a typo. Repeated failures or a sudden change in device give the administrator more context about what to investigate.

Walk from left to right. React is the interface. Spring Boot checks permissions and runs the application logic. PostgreSQL stores the evidence. Grok or the fallback planner can assist when someone asks a question.

Follow a single sign-in. Spring Boot checks the credentials, attempts to store the event and evaluates the rules. Saving telemetry in a separate transaction helps preserve evidence when authentication fails.
Use one rule to illustrate the table, such as a new IP adding 40 points. Multiple rules can match the same event. The severity shown here belongs to the rule match.
Read the example aloud. Twenty plus forty plus thirty equals ninety, so the account is Critical. Older alerts stop contributing after 24 hours. The weights are fixed priorities.

Use the example prompt ‘Summarize recent alerts.’ The assistant can query authorized records and show its tool steps. In the implementation, the outer loop handles supplied follow-ups and the inner loop handles tool calls.
A user sees their own activity. Administrators can review across accounts and decide whether to change account status. The backend checks authorization and records administrative actions.

Read the three headline numbers and explain that 26 out of 32 sessions failed in the demonstration view. These figures describe the captured demo state. The thesis lists controlled evaluation as future validation.
Close with the part of the project you can demonstrate end to end: how a login produces evidence for an account decision. Mention the validation work you would run next, then invite questions.
